arc_intro:
FQ-171 — Ravi Krishnan (Head of Engineering)

This fleet grows and shrinks based on someone noticing traffic is high and manually bumping a number, not on any automatic policy. order-service's ASG has had min=3, desired=4, max=6 since the resilience work a while back, but nobody ever actually attached a scaling policy to it. Let's fix that properly, and let's make sure the numbers themselves are actually right, not just present.

— Ravi
arc_outro:
Ravi Krishnan — FQ-171 update:

Good instinct catching that max=6 during the flash sale test — a real scaling policy is only as good as the ceiling it's allowed to work within. Target tracking is live now, cooldowns are sensible, and max is raised to something that can actually absorb a real spike instead of hitting a wall and returning 503s to customers.

Last piece of compute: pricing models. We've been paying On-Demand for everything, and I don't think that's right for all of it.

— Ravi

tasks.question: What's the difference between target tracking scaling, step scaling, and scheduled scaling?
options: A) They're three names for the exact same underlying mechanism, just configured through different console screens

B) Target tracking automatically adjusts capacity to keep a metric (e.g. CPU utilization) at a set target, continuously and reactively. C) Scheduled scaling is deprecated and should never be used in any modern setup
D) Step scaling can only scale IN (remove instances), never scale OUT (add instances)

tasks.scenario: Historical data shows CPU utilization climbing above 80% is when latency actually starts degrading for customers. karthik-dev suggests setting the target tracking target at 85%, reasoning 'that way we use the instances more fully before scaling out, saving cost.'
tasks.question: Is targeting 85% CPU utilization a good choice here?
options: A) Yes — maximizing utilization before scaling always saves the most money with no downside

B) No — since 80% is where degradation actually starts, a target of 85% means the ASG only starts scaling out AFTER customers are already experiencing problems, and it takes time to actually launch and register new instances. The target should be set with headroom BELOW the degradation point (e.g. 60-65%), so scaling completes before customers are affected, not after
C) Yes, but only if the cooldown period is also set to zero
D) It doesn't matter what target is chosen, since target tracking always scales instantly with zero lag

tasks.scenario: The target tracking policy is live and working well for weeks. Then FoodQuick runs a major flash sale promotion, driving traffic far higher than anything seen before. Customers start reporting 503 errors during the sale's peak hour.
tasks.error_shown: ALB target group: "503 Service Unavailable" — CloudWatch shows the ASG at 6/6 instances (at max capacity) with CPU utilization at 94%, scaling activity log shows repeated 'attempted to scale to 8 desired, but max capacity is 6' entries
tasks.diagnosis: The target tracking policy is working exactly as designed — it correctly detected sustained high CPU and repeatedly tried to scale out. But it hit the ASG's max=6 ceiling, which was set during the earlier resilience work for a very different reason (AZ-failure redundancy) and was never revisited for genuine peak-traffic capacity planning. The policy has no ability to exceed max, no matter how badly it's needed — max is a hard ceiling by design.
tasks.fix: Raise the ASG's max capacity to a value that reflects genuine peak-traffic headroom (informed by load testing, not just AZ-redundancy math), and re-run a simulated flash-sale-level load test to confirm the new max allows the policy to scale out enough to avoid 503s.

cases.case_1: order-service's day-to-day, somewhat unpredictable customer traffic, which needs to respond automatically to whatever load actually shows up
cases.case_2: FoodQuick's known, reliable daily lunch-hour (12-2pm) traffic spike, which happens predictably every single day regardless of anything else

correct_answers.case_1: Target tracking — reactive, continuous adjustment fits genuinely unpredictable day-to-day load best
correct_answers.case_2: Scheduled scaling (as a baseline floor before lunch hour) combined with target tracking as the safety net on top — since the pattern is known and reliable, pre-scaling ahead of it avoids any lag, while target tracking still handles anything beyond the expected pattern
correct_answers.case_3: Scheduled scaling for the specific known event, likely combined with a temporarily raised max capacity for that window specifically, similar to the flash-sale lesson just learned

tasks.scenario: Ravi asks whether raising max from 6 to 12 creates a meaningful ongoing cost risk, given the ASG could theoretically now run twice as many instances. An m5.large costs roughly ₹5,600/month running continuously; the target tracking policy only scales OUT when actual CPU load genuinely demands it, and back in when load subsides.
tasks.question: Is raising max to 12 a meaningful ongoing cost risk, given how target tracking actually works?
tasks.solution: Raising max doesn't mean FoodQuick pays for 12 instances constantly — the target tracking policy only scales toward max when genuine load actually requires it, and scales back down afterward. The real cost exposure is bounded by actual usage patterns, not the ceiling itself. The flash-sale test showed peak usage around 10 instances for a few hours, not 12 for a whole month — a realistic cost impact of a few thousand rupees for that event, which is a reasonable trade against the 503-driven lost sales and customer trust the last flash sale actually cost.
